g.text: World models that predict environment dynamics have emerged as a
powerful tool for agent decision-making (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018;
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=2) World models that predict environment dynamics have emerged as a powerful tool for agent decision-making (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Schrittwieser et al., 2019).

g.text: For agents operating in environments with irreversible
actions—such as submitting purchases, sending emails, or deleting
files—world models can serve as pre-execution verifiers: before
committing to a high-stakes action, the agent queries…
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=0) For agents operating in environments with irreversible actions—such as submitting purchases, sending emails, or deleting files—world models can serve as pre-execution verifiers: before committing to a high-stakes action, the agent queries the world model to predict whether the action will succeed.

g.text: LLM world models verify web checkout
Recent work has demonstrated this approach for web agents, using LLM-based
world models to verify checkout actions before execution (Li et al., 2025;
g.title: N3 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) Recent work has demonstrated this approach for web agents, using LLM-based world models to verify checkout actions before execution (Li et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025).

g.text: However, a counterintuitive failure mode has been observed: increasing the
verification budget (the number of world-model queries allowed) can reduce
g.title: N4 [Limitation] (cites=1) However, a counterintuitive failure mode has been observed: increasing the verification budget (the number of world-model queries allowed) can reduce task success rates (Li et al., 2025).

g.text: This nonmonotonic behavior occurs because sequential verify-and-retry
g.title: N5 [Limitation] (cites=0) This nonmonotonic behavior occurs because sequential verify-and-retry creates a problematic feedback loop.

g.text: When verification rejects a checkout (potentially a false negative), the
agent re-browses to find another product.
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) When verification rejects a checkout (potentially a false negative), the agent re-browses to find another product.

g.text: During re-browsing, the agent often selects a worse product than the one
originally found—a phenomenon we call trajectory drift.
g.title: N7 [Limitation] (cites=0) During re-browsing, the agent often selects a worse product than the one originally found—a phenomenon we call trajectory drift.

g.text: More verification cycles mean more opportunities for trajectory drift.
g.title: N8 [Limitation] (cites=0) More verification cycles mean more opportunities for trajectory drift.

g.text: The key insight is that the problem lies not in verification
accuracy, but in the sequential structure of verify-and-retry.
g.title: N9 [Context] (cites=0) The key insight is that the problem lies not in verification accuracy, but in the sequential structure of verify-and-retry.

g.text: Each rejection triggers re-browsing, compounding errors across
g.title: N10 [Context] (cites=0) Each rejection triggers re-browsing, compounding errors across cycles.

g.text: Solution: fewer cycles, more parallel rollouts
This suggests a simple solution: instead of spreading the verification
budget across many sequential cycles, spend it in fewer cycles with more
g.title: N11 [Context] (cites=0) This suggests a simple solution: instead of spreading the verification budget across many sequential cycles, spend it in fewer cycles with more parallel rollouts per cycle.

g.text: We propose chunked budget allocation: given a fixed verification budget B,
allocate it across M cycles with K = B/M parallel world-model rollouts per
g.title: N12 [Method] (cites=0) We propose chunked budget allocation: given a fixed verification budget B, allocate it across M cycles with K = B/M parallel world-model rollouts per cycle.

g.text: M=1: one parallel chunk eliminates drift
By setting M = 1, we spend the entire budget in one parallel chunk,
eliminating the sequential cycles that trigger trajectory drift.
g.title: N13 [Method] (cites=0) By setting M = 1, we spend the entire budget in one parallel chunk, eliminating the sequential cycles that trigger trajectory drift.

g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We identify trajectory drift as the dominant failure mode in sequential verify-and-retry, accounting for 60.5% of failures when agents re-browse after verification rejection.

g.text: We demonstrate that chunked budget allocation achieves
a 25× improvement in task success rate (21.50% vs.
g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We demonstrate that chunked budget allocation achieves a 25× improvement in task success rate (21.50% vs. 0.86%) by eliminating sequential verification cycles.

g.text: C3: consensus has no benefit (98.4% miscalib)
We show that consensus aggregation across parallel
rollouts provides no benefit over single-rollout
acceptance, as the world model's poor calibration
g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We show that consensus aggregation across parallel rollouts provides no benefit over single-rollout acceptance, as the world model's poor calibration (predicting p̂ = 0 for 98.4% of cycles) causes consensus to degenerate.

g.text: We provide practical guidance: setting M = 1 (spending
all budget in one parallel chunk) consistently
g.title: C4 [Contribution] (cites=0) We provide practical guidance: setting M = 1 (spending all budget in one parallel chunk) consistently outperforms finer-grained allocations, with performance degrading monotonically as M increases.
